key_terms.meaning: A substance with one fixed chemical composition throughout, e.g. water, nitrogen; it may exist in more than one phase but each phase has the same composition
Liquid at a pressure above the saturation pressure for its temperature; also called subcooled liquid
Liquid exactly at the boiling point for its pressure, with no vapour present, quality x = 0
Vapour exactly at the boiling point for its pressure, just about to condense, quality x = 1
Vapour at a temperature higher than the saturation temperature for its pressure
The surface in p-v-T space on which every equilibrium state of a pure substance lies; single-phase sheets and two-phase ruled surfaces, with the triple line where three two-phase surfaces meet
The single pressure and temperature at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium; for water 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa
The end point of the liquid-vapour saturation curve; for water 647.1 K (374 °C) and 220.6 bar, where latent heat falls to zero
F = C − P + 2 for a non-reacting system in equilibrium; for a pure substance F = 3 − P, so at most three phases coexist
Heat absorbed by 1 kg of saturated liquid to become saturated vapour at constant pressure and temperature, h<sub>fg</sub> = h<sub>g</sub> − h<sub>f</sub>
x = mass of dry vapour ÷ total mass of wet mixture, so 0 ≤ x ≤ 1; x = 0 saturated liquid, x = 1 saturated vapour
Tabulated values of h<sub>f</sub>, h<sub>g</sub>, h<sub>fg</sub>, v<sub>f</sub>, v<sub>g</sub>, s<sub>f</sub> and s<sub>g</sub> against pressure and temperature for water and steam
An h-s diagram of steam on which isobars, isotherms, constant-x lines and constant-v lines are drawn, used for graphical reading of properties and processes
A device that throttles wet steam to a low pressure so it becomes superheated; h before equals h after, which gives x
A gas whose molecules occupy no volume and exert no forces except during collision; obeys pv = RT with R = R<sub>u</sub>/M

(p + a/v²)(v − b) = R<sub>u</sub>T with v the molar volume; a corrects for attraction and b for molecular volume; a = 27R<sub>u</sub>²T<sub>c</sub>²/(64p<sub>c</sub>), b = R<sub>u</sub>T<sub>c</sub>/(8p<sub>c</sub>)
Z = pv/RT; Z = 1 for an ideal gas, and departure from 1 measures the error of the ideal gas approximation
For an ideal gas mixture the total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures: p = Σp<sub>i</sub>, with p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub> p
y<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>/n = N<sub>i</sub>/N, the number of moles of component i divided by the total moles in the mixture
w = m<sub>v</sub>/m<sub>a</sub> = 0.622 p<sub>v</sub>/(p − p<sub>v</sub>), kilograms of water vapour carried by 1 kg of dry air
A plot of moist air properties — dry-bulb temperature, humidity ratio, relative humidity, enthalpy — from which the state point gives all the others

takeaways: All equilibrium states of a pure substance lie on its p-v-T surface, and the two-phase region is only a surface or a line, not a volume.
The triple point is a single point for a given substance; the critical point closes the liquid-vapour curve and removes the difference between liquid and vapour.
The Gibbs phase rule F = C − P + 2 counts the free intensive properties: two for one phase of water, one on a saturation curve, none at the triple point.
Inside the wet region pressure and temperature are not independent — fixing one fixes the other, so a second property such as x is needed to fix the state.
Enthalpy of wet steam follows h = h<sub>f</sub> + x·h<sub>fg</sub>, and the same mixing rule applies to v, s and u with v<sub>f</sub>, v<sub>g</sub> and s<sub>f</sub>, s<sub>g</sub>.
Steam tables and the Mollier chart are read, not solved; they replace the missing equation of state for water in exam problems.
A throttling calorimeter relies on the fact that h is constant across a throttle, and it works only when the steam is dry enough to leave superheated.
Real gases depart from pv = RT near saturation and at high pressure; Z = pv/RT, read from the generalised chart with reduced properties, quantifies that departure.
In an ideal gas mixture each component behaves as if alone in the vessel, so the mixture calculations reduce to weighted sums using mole fractions.
Moist air is treated as an ideal gas mixture of dry air and water vapour, which is why the psychrometric chart carries two independent temperatures.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are almost always numerical plus a diagram: a labelled p-v, T-v, p-T or h-s sketch with the tables actually read to produce h, v, s and Z. Most syllabi expect the method and the numbers together, not one without the other.

bank.q: Draw the p-v-T surface of water and explain what every region and every line on it represents. Show how the p-v and T-v diagrams are obtained from it as projections.
outline: Solid, liquid and vapour single-phase sheets joined by three two-phase ruled surfaces
The triple line, where the three two-phase surfaces meet, projects to the triple point on the p-T plane
Fusion surface of water tilts because water expands on freezing
Vaporisation surface ends at the critical point; beyond it liquid and vapour cannot be told apart
Sublimation surface lies below the triple line
Lines of constant T and constant p on the surface become the isotherms and isobars of the p-v and T-v diagrams
answer: Why a surface: by the state postulate, two independent intensive properties fix the state of a simple compressible substance, so p = f(v, T). Every equilibrium state of water is one point on a single surface in p-v-T space.
Single-phase sheets: solid, liquid and vapour. The liquid sheet is steep, because liquid hardly changes volume with pressure; the vapour sheet at large v flattens towards the ideal-gas form pv = RT.

Two-phase surfaces: solid–liquid (fusion), liquid–vapour (vaporisation) and solid–vapour (sublimation). Each is a ruled surface made of straight lines parallel to the v axis, because p and T stay fixed while the share of the phases, and so v, changes. At 1 atm the liquid–vapour line runs from v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 to v<sub>g</sub> = 1.673 m³/kg at 100 °C.
Triple line: the three two-phase surfaces meet along one line at 0.01 °C and 0.6117 kPa. Along it ice, liquid and vapour coexist; only v changes, between the saturated volumes of the three phases.
Critical point: the liquid–vapour surface narrows as pressure rises and closes at 373.95 °C, 22.064 MPa and v<sub>c</sub> = 0.003106 m³/kg. Above it there is no boiling; the fluid is supercritical.

Water’s special feature: ice (v ≈ 0.00109 m³/kg) is less dense than liquid (0.00100 m³/kg), so water expands on freezing. The fusion surface therefore leans so that its p-T line has a negative slope: more pressure lowers the melting point slightly.

answer.text: Projections. Looking along the v axis, each two-phase surface is seen edge-on, so it becomes a line on the p-T plane and the triple line becomes the triple point. Looking along the T axis gives the p-v diagram below; looking along the p axis gives the T-v diagram.

answer: T-v projection: the same dome appears; a constant-pressure line rises through liquid, runs flat at T<sub>sat</sub> across the dome and rises again in vapour, as in Figure 5.1.1.

Check with numbers: at 1 atm the wet region is v<sub>g</sub>/v<sub>f</sub> = 1.673/0.001043 ≈ 1604 times wide in v, while at the critical point the width is zero; this is why the dome looks so lopsided and is usually drawn with a log v axis.

bank.q: Define triple point and critical point. Give their values for water and explain why the liquid-vapour saturation curve ends at the critical point.
outline: Triple point: unique (p, T) where solid, liquid and vapour coexist; water 273.16 K, 0.6117 kPa
Critical point: highest (p, T) at which liquid and vapour are distinct; water 647.1 K, 22.064 MPa
Latent heat of vaporisation falls to zero at the critical point
Densities of the two phases become equal and surface tension vanishes
Above the critical temperature a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone
answer: Triple point: the one state at which solid, liquid and vapour of a pure substance coexist in equilibrium. By the phase rule F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0, so it has no free property. For water: T = 273.16 K (0.01 °C) and p = 0.6117 kPa.

Critical point: the highest temperature and pressure at which liquid and vapour can exist as two distinct phases. For water: T<sub>c</sub> = 647.1 K (373.95 °C), p<sub>c</sub> = 22.064 MPa, v<sub>c</sub> = 0.003106 m³/kg (density 322 kg/m³).

answer.text: How the two phases approach each other as pressure rises (steam tables):

answer: Why the curve ends: as T rises the liquid expands and the vapour is compressed, so their densities move together. At the critical point v<sub>f</sub> = v<sub>g</sub>, h<sub>fg</sub> = 0 and the surface tension that separates the two phases vanishes. With no difference left between them, there is nothing for a boiling curve to separate.

On the p-v diagram the critical isotherm has a horizontal inflection there: (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = 0 and (∂²p/∂v²)<sub>T</sub> = 0. Below T<sub>c</sub> isotherms have a flat two-phase stretch; above T<sub>c</sub> they have none.

Consequence: above T<sub>c</sub> no pressure, however high, produces a separate liquid. Water at 700 K and 25 MPa, for example, is a supercritical fluid; supercritical boilers use this to avoid a boiling stage.

The triple point, by contrast, is the lower end of the boiling curve: below 0.6117 kPa there is no liquid, and ice sublimes. Carbon dioxide’s triple point is at 518 kPa, which is why dry ice sublimes at 1 atm.

Check: the critical compressibility of water is Z<sub>c</sub> = p<sub>c</sub>v<sub>c</sub>/(RT<sub>c</sub>) = 22 064 × 0.003106/(0.4615 × 647.1) = 68.53/298.6 = 0.229, far below 1, which shows how far from ideal water is at its critical point.

bank.q: Explain the formation of steam at constant pressure from 0 °C water to superheated steam. Show the process on a T-h and an h-s diagram, and define sensible heat, latent heat, dryness fraction and degree of superheat.
outline: Sensible heating of liquid from 0 °C to saturation temperature, h<sub>f</sub>
Evaporation at constant temperature absorbing h<sub>fg</sub>
Superheating of vapour, extra enthalpy h − h<sub>g</sub>
Dryness fraction x marks the position along the evaporation line
Degree of superheat = T − T<sub>sat</sub> at the given pressure
Diagrams: liquid line, evaporation line, superheat region with isobars for two pressures
answer: Set-up: 1 kg of water at 0 °C in a cylinder whose piston keeps the pressure at 10 bar. Heat is added slowly. Steam tables take h ≈ 0 for water at 0 °C (about 1 kJ/kg at 10 bar).

Stage 1, sensible heat of the liquid: the temperature rises from 0 °C to T<sub>sat</sub> = 179.9 °C. The heat added is h<sub>f</sub> − 0 = 762.5 kJ/kg (a check with c ≈ 4.19 kJ/(kg·K): 4.19 × 179.9 ≈ 754 kJ/kg). Sensible heat is heat that changes temperature without changing phase.

Stage 2, latent heat: at 179.9 °C the water boils; the temperature stays fixed while h<sub>fg</sub> = 2014.6 kJ/kg is added. Latent heat is heat that changes phase at constant temperature and pressure.

Dryness fraction during stage 2: x = m<sub>g</sub>/(m<sub>f</sub> + m<sub>g</sub>), from 0 (saturated liquid) to 1 (dry saturated steam). Any point on the boiling line has h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub>; for x = 0.9, h = 762.5 + 0.9 × 2014.6 = 2575.6 kJ/kg.
At x = 1 the steam is dry saturated: h<sub>g</sub> = 762.5 + 2014.6 = 2777.1 kJ/kg.

Stage 3, superheat: further heat raises the temperature of the vapour. At 250 °C the superheated table gives h = 2943.1 kJ/kg. Degree of superheat = T − T<sub>sat</sub> = 250 − 179.9 = 70.1 K; heat of superheat = 2943.1 − 2777.1 = 166.0 kJ/kg.

answer.text: Summary of the heat per kg at 10 bar:

answer: T-h diagram (Figure 5.4.1): a sloped liquid line up to (762.5 kJ/kg, 179.9 °C), a flat boiling line 2014.6 kJ/kg long, then a rising superheat line. At 1 atm the flat line is lower (100 °C) and longer (2257 kJ/kg); it shrinks to a point at the critical pressure.

h-s diagram (Figure 5.5.1): inside the dome the 10 bar isobar is a straight line whose slope dh/ds equals T<sub>sat</sub> = 453 K; past the saturated vapour line it curves upward and steepens. The x = 0.9 state lies on the straight part; the 250 °C state lies on the curved part.
Check: 762.5 + 2014.6 + 166.0 = 2943.1 kJ/kg, the table value at 10 bar and 250 °C, so the three stages account for all the heat.

bank.q: State Dalton's law of partial pressures and Amagat's law of additive volumes. For an ideal gas mixture show that the mole fraction equals the volume fraction and that p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>·p.
outline: Dalton: p = Σp<sub>i</sub> with each gas at the mixture volume and temperature
Amagat: V = ΣV<sub>i</sub> with each gas at the mixture pressure and temperature
Ideal gas for each component: p<sub>i</sub>V = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T
Divide the component equation by the mixture equation to get p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p
Volume fraction V<sub>i</sub>/V equals n<sub>i</sub>/n = y<sub>i</sub>
Valid only for ideal gas mixtures at moderate pressure
answer: Dalton’s law: the pressure of a mixture of ideal gases equals the sum of the partial pressures, p = Σ p<sub>i</sub>, where p<sub>i</sub> is the pressure gas i would exert if it alone filled the whole volume V at the mixture temperature T.

Amagat’s law: the volume of the mixture equals the sum of the partial volumes, V = Σ V<sub>i</sub>, where V<sub>i</sub> is the volume gas i would occupy alone at the mixture pressure p and temperature T.
Mixture as a whole: pV = nR<sub>u</sub>T with n = Σ n<sub>i</sub>. Component i in Dalton’s picture: p<sub>i</sub>V = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T.

Divide: p<sub>i</sub>/p = (n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T/V)/(nR<sub>u</sub>T/V) = n<sub>i</sub>/n = y<sub>i</sub>. So p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p, and adding over i gives Σ p<sub>i</sub> = p Σ y<sub>i</sub> = p, which is Dalton’s law.

Component i in Amagat’s picture: pV<sub>i</sub> = n<sub>i</sub>R<sub>u</sub>T. Dividing by pV = nR<sub>u</sub>T gives V<sub>i</sub>/V = n<sub>i</sub>/n = y<sub>i</sub>: the volume fraction equals the mole fraction. Adding gives Σ V<sub>i</sub> = V.
So for ideal gases p<sub>i</sub>/p = V<sub>i</sub>/V = y<sub>i</sub>. A gas analysis by volume (such as an Orsat analysis) is therefore also an analysis by moles.

answer.text: Numerical check with the tank of the gas-mixture chapter (0.8 kg O₂ and 2.8 kg N₂ in 2 m³ at 300 K):

answer: The mass fraction is different: w<sub>O2</sub> = 0.8/3.6 = 0.222, not 0.2. Putting mass fractions into p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p is the commonest error.
Validity: both laws assume ideal gases with no forces between unlike molecules. At high pressure (hundreds of bar) or near condensation they fail and Z with Kay’s pseudocritical values is needed.
Check: 31.2 + 124.7 = 155.9 kPa and 0.4 + 1.6 = 2.0 m³, so both laws close on the example.

bank.q: Steam at 10 bar has a dryness fraction of 0.90. Using steam tables (h<sub>f</sub> = 762.5 kJ/kg, h<sub>fg</sub> = 2014.6 kJ/kg, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001127 m³/kg, v<sub>g</sub> = 0.1944 m³/kg, s<sub>f</sub> = 2.1381, s<sub>fg</sub> = 4.4470 kJ/kg·K) find h, v, u and s of 1 kg.
outline: h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> = 2575.6 kJ/kg
v = v<sub>f</sub> + x (v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>) = 0.1751 m³/kg
u = h − p·v with p in kPa = 2400.6 kJ/kg
s = s<sub>f</sub> + x s<sub>fg</sub> = 6.1404 kJ/kg·K
v<sub>f</sub> is small but not zero, and u is not h
answer: Given: p = 10 bar = 1000 kPa, x = 0.90, so the steam is wet and its temperature is T<sub>sat</sub> = 179.9 °C. All f and g values are at 10 bar.
The shortcut v ≈ x v<sub>g</sub> = 0.90 × 0.1944 = 0.17496 m³/kg is only 0.06 per cent low here, but it fails at small x, where x v<sub>g</sub> can be less than v<sub>f</sub> itself.
Cross-check u another way: tables give u<sub>f</sub> = 761.4 and u<sub>g</sub> = 2582.7 kJ/kg at 10 bar, so u = 761.4 + 0.90 × (2582.7 − 761.4) = 761.4 + 1639.2 = 2400.6 kJ/kg, the same value.
Check: h lies between h<sub>f</sub> = 762.5 and h<sub>g</sub> = 2777.1 kJ/kg, and s between s<sub>f</sub> = 2.1381 and s<sub>g</sub> = 6.5850 kJ/kg·K, as a wet state must.

bank.q: Steam at 8 bar passes through a throttling calorimeter and leaves at 1 bar, 120 °C. Using h<sub>f</sub> = 720.9 kJ/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2047.4 kJ/kg at 8 bar, and h = 2716.6 kJ/kg for steam at 1 bar, 120 °C, find the dryness fraction of the main steam.
outline: Throttling is adiabatic with no work, so h₁ = h₂
h₂ = 2716.6 kJ/kg from the superheated table at 1 bar, 120 °C
h₁ = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> = 720.9 + x × 2047.4
State the assumptions: steady flow, negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, no heat loss
answer: Steady flow energy equation for the throttle, per kg: q − w = (h₂ − h₁) + (c₂² − c₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁). The valve does no work (w = 0), the insulated body loses little heat (q ≈ 0), and the velocity and height changes are small, so h₁ = h₂.
Outlet state: at 1 bar T<sub>sat</sub> = 99.6 °C. The outlet is at 120 °C, so it is superheated by 20.4 K, and p₂ and T₂ fix h₂ = 2716.6 kJ/kg from the table.
Inlet: wet steam at 8 bar, h₁ = h<sub>f</sub> + x₁ h<sub>fg</sub> = 720.9 + 2047.4 x₁.
Meaning: each kg of main steam carries 0.975 kg of vapour and 0.025 kg of water droplets.

Validity check: the outlet is just dry when h₂ = h<sub>g</sub>(1 bar) = 2675.0 kJ/kg, which would need x₁ = (2675.0 − 720.9)/2047.4 = 0.954. Our x₁ = 0.975 is above that, so a superheated outlet is consistent.
Sensitivity: near 1 bar and 120 °C, h changes by about 2.0 kJ/kg per K, so a 1 K error in T₂ changes x₁ by 2.0/2047.4 ≈ 0.001. A good thermometer is therefore enough.
Back-substitution: h₁ = 720.9 + 0.9748 × 2047.4 = 720.9 + 1995.8 = 2716.7 kJ/kg ≈ 2716.6, so the answer closes.
Answer: x₁ ≈ 0.975 (97.5 per cent dry).

bank.q: One kilogram of carbon dioxide is held in a 0.05 m³ vessel at 300 K. Calculate the pressure using (i) the ideal gas equation and (ii) the van der Waals equation (a = 364.3 kPa·m⁶/kmol², b = 0.0427 m³/kmol), and comment on the difference.
outline: n = 1/44 kmol
Ideal: p = nR<sub>u</sub>T/V ≈ 1133.7 kPa
van der Waals: p = nR<sub>u</sub>T/(V − nb) − a n²/V²
nb = 0.00097 m³, so the first term ≈ 1156.2 kPa
Attraction term ≈ 75.3 kPa, giving p ≈ 1080.9 kPa
Real pressure is below ideal because attraction dominates at this moderate density
answer: Amount: n = m/M = 1/44 = 0.022727 kmol. R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K), and the units kPa, m³ and kmol go together.
van der Waals for n kmol: p = nR<sub>u</sub>T/(V − nb) − an²/V².
van der Waals pressure: p = 1156.2 − 75.3 = 1080.9 kPa.

head: Method
p (kPa)
vs ideal
rows: Reference data for CO₂ at this state

answer: Comment: the molecular-volume correction raises p by 22.5 kPa, the attraction correction lowers it by 75.3 kPa, so attraction wins and the real pressure is below ideal. The effective Z = 1080.9/1133.7 = 0.953.
Check: van der Waals lands within 0.8 per cent of the reference value 1072.2 kPa, while the ideal law is 5.7 per cent high, which is the expected ranking at this moderate density (20 kg/m³).

bank.q: A gas mixture has the volumetric analysis CO₂ 12%, O₂ 8%, N₂ 80%. For the mixture find the molar mass, the gas constant, the mass fractions, the partial pressure of each gas at 1 bar and 300 K, and the density.
outline: Mass fraction w<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub>/M
p<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>p: CO₂ 0.12 bar, O₂ 0.08 bar, N₂ 0.80 bar
Density ρ = p/(RT)
Volume fraction = mole fraction for an ideal gas mixture
answer: For ideal gases a volumetric analysis is a mole analysis, so y<sub>CO2</sub> = 0.12, y<sub>O2</sub> = 0.08 and y<sub>N2</sub> = 0.80 (sum 1.00).
Gas constant: R = R<sub>u</sub>/M = 8.314/30.24 = 0.2749 kJ/(kg·K).
Partial pressures at p = 1 bar: p<sub>CO2</sub> = 0.12 bar, p<sub>O2</sub> = 0.08 bar, p<sub>N2</sub> = 0.80 bar.
Note that CO₂ is 12 per cent by volume but 17.5 per cent by mass, because its molecules are heavier than the mixture average.
Check: the mass fractions add to 0.1746 + 0.0847 + 0.7407 = 1.0000 and the partial pressures to 1.00 bar.

bank.q: Moist air at 1 atm has a dry-bulb temperature of 30 °C and a wet-bulb temperature of 20 °C. Find the humidity ratio, relative humidity, dew-point temperature, specific enthalpy and specific volume, and say how the chart confirms them.
outline: Saturated humidity ratio at the wet-bulb temperature
Adiabatic saturation balance gives w ≈ 0.0105 kg/kg dry air
p<sub>v</sub> from w, then φ ≈ 40 %
Dew point where p<sub>sat</sub> = p<sub>v</sub>, about 14.8 °C
v = R<sub>a</sub>T/p<sub>a</sub> ≈ 0.873 m³/kg dry air
answer: Data from steam tables: p<sub>sat</sub>(20 °C) = 2.339 kPa, p<sub>sat</sub>(30 °C) = 4.247 kPa, h<sub>fg</sub>(20 °C) = 2453.5 kJ/kg, h<sub>f</sub>(20 °C) = 83.9 kJ/kg, h<sub>g</sub>(30 °C) = 2555.6 kJ/kg; p = 101.325 kPa.
Air saturated at the wet-bulb temperature: w₂ = 0.622 × 2.339/(101.325 − 2.339) = 1.4549/98.986 = 0.014698 kg/kg.

Adiabatic saturation balance (the wet-bulb temperature taken as the adiabatic saturation temperature): w₁ = [c<sub>p</sub>(T₂ − T₁) + w₂h<sub>fg2</sub>]/(h<sub>g1</sub> − h<sub>f2</sub>) = [1.005 × (20 − 30) + 0.014698 × 2453.5]/(2555.6 − 83.9) = (−10.05 + 36.06)/2471.7 = 0.01052 kg/kg dry air.
Vapour pressure: p<sub>v</sub> = w p/(0.622 + w) = 0.01052 × 101.325/0.63252 = 1.686 kPa. Relative humidity: φ = 1.686/4.247 = 0.397, about 40 per cent.
Specific volume: v = R<sub>a</sub>T/p<sub>a</sub> = 0.287 × 303.15/(101.325 − 1.686) = 87.00/99.64 = 0.873 m³/kg dry air.

On the chart: the 20 °C wet-bulb line meets the 30 °C dry-bulb line at a point between the 30 % and 50 % curves; reading across gives w ≈ 0.0105 and left to saturation gives about 15 °C, which confirms the numbers.
Check of order: T<sub>dp</sub> = 14.8 °C < T<sub>wb</sub> = 20 °C < T<sub>db</sub> = 30 °C, as it must be for unsaturated air.

bank.q: Explain physically why a real gas deviates from pv = RT. Derive the van der Waals constants a and b in terms of critical properties and show how the equation predicts the critical point.
outline: Two assumptions break down: molecules have finite volume, and they attract each other
b corrects the volume, a/v² corrects the pressure
At the critical point the isotherm has an inflection: (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = 0 and (∂²p/∂v²)<sub>T</sub> = 0
Solving gives v<sub>c</sub> = 3b, T<sub>c</sub> = 8a/(27Rb), p<sub>c</sub> = a/(27b²)
Therefore a = 27R²T<sub>c</sub>²/(64p<sub>c</sub>) and b = RT<sub>c</sub>/(8p<sub>c</sub>)
Predicted Z<sub>c</sub> = 3/8 = 0.375 for all substances, against about 0.23 to 0.29 measured
answer: Why real gases deviate: the ideal model treats molecules as points that do not attract. At high density both assumptions fail. Molecules fill part of the volume, so the free volume is less than v (this raises p), and neighbours pull a molecule back as it approaches the wall (this lowers p).
van der Waals’ corrections, per mole: replace v by (v − b) and add a/v² to the measured pressure: (p + a/v²)(v − b) = RT, or p = RT/(v − b) − a/v².
Critical conditions: the critical isotherm has a horizontal inflection at the critical point, so (∂p/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = 0 and (∂²p/∂v²)<sub>T</sub> = 0 there.
From (1): RT = 2a(v − b)²/v³. Put this in (2): 4a/[v³(v − b)] = 6a/v⁴, so 4v = 6(v − b) and v<sub>c</sub> = 3b.
Then RT<sub>c</sub> = 2a(2b)²/(27b³) = 8a/(27b), so T<sub>c</sub> = 8a/(27Rb).
And p<sub>c</sub> = RT<sub>c</sub>/(v<sub>c</sub> − b) − a/v<sub>c</sub>² = [8a/(27b)]/(2b) − a/(9b²) = 4a/(27b²) − 3a/(27b²) = a/(27b²).

Solve for the constants from the measured T<sub>c</sub> and p<sub>c</sub>: from T<sub>c</sub>/p<sub>c</sub> = 8b/R, b = RT<sub>c</sub>/(8p<sub>c</sub>); then a = 27b²p<sub>c</sub> = 27R²T<sub>c</sub>²/(64p<sub>c</sub>).

Predicted critical compressibility: Z<sub>c</sub> = p<sub>c</sub>v<sub>c</sub>/(RT<sub>c</sub>) = [a/(27b²)] × 3b/[8a/(27b)] = 3/8 = 0.375 for every gas. Measured values are lower (0.29 for nitrogen, 0.27 for CO₂, 0.23 for water), a known weakness of the two-constant equation near the critical point.
Check: putting the CO₂ values back, T<sub>c</sub> = 8a/(27Rb) = 8 × 0.3654/(27 × 8.314 × 4.28 × 10⁻⁵) = 2.923/0.009608 = 304.2 K, which returns the critical temperature.

bank.q: A throttling calorimeter reads reliably only when the main steam is fairly dry. Explain why, find the limit for steam at 10 bar throttled to 1 bar, and describe how a combined separating and throttling calorimeter extends the range.
outline: After throttling the steam must be superheated, otherwise its state is still two-phase and its enthalpy cannot be found from temperature alone
Limit: h₁ = h<sub>g</sub>(p₂) gives the smallest readable x₁
Separating calorimeter removes most of the water mechanically and gives x<sub>s</sub> from the masses
The nearly dry steam is then throttled and x<sub>t</sub> found by the enthalpy balance
Overall x = x<sub>s</sub> × x<sub>t</sub>
answer: Principle: throttling keeps h constant, h₁ = h₂. The measured outlet p₂ and T₂ give h₂ only if the outlet is superheated; if it is still wet, T₂ is just T<sub>sat</sub>(p₂) and tells nothing about h₂.

Limit: the wettest steam that can still leave dry has h₁ = h<sub>g</sub>(p₂). For p₂ = 1 bar, h<sub>g</sub> = 2675.0 kJ/kg; at p₁ = 10 bar, h<sub>f</sub> = 762.5 and h<sub>fg</sub> = 2014.6 kJ/kg, so x<sub>1,min</sub> = (2675.0 − 762.5)/2014.6 = 0.949.

answer.text: The limit at other inlet pressures (outlet 1 bar):

answer: So a throttling calorimeter alone can only test steam drier than about 95 per cent at these pressures. Wetter steam would need a much lower outlet pressure, which is not practical.

Separating calorimeter: baffles turn the sample sharply, droplets strike the walls and drain into a gauge glass; the steam that passes is condensed and weighed. With m<sub>w</sub> water separated and m<sub>s</sub> steam passed, x<sub>s</sub> = m<sub>s</sub>/(m<sub>s</sub> + m<sub>w</sub>). Fine droplets escape, so x<sub>s</sub> alone overstates the dryness.
Combined unit: the separator removes most of the water first, so the steam leaving it is dry enough for the throttling part, which then measures its dryness x<sub>t</sub>.

Overall dryness: vapour in the sample = x<sub>t</sub> m<sub>s</sub>; total mass = m<sub>s</sub> + m<sub>w</sub>; so x = x<sub>t</sub> m<sub>s</sub>/(m<sub>s</sub> + m<sub>w</sub>) = x<sub>s</sub> × x<sub>t</sub>.

Example: 0.5 kg separated and 9.5 kg passed, throttled outlet 1 bar and 130 °C (h₂ = 2736.7 kJ/kg). x<sub>s</sub> = 9.5/10 = 0.95; x<sub>t</sub> = (2736.7 − 762.5)/2014.6 = 0.980; x = 0.95 × 0.980 = 0.931.
Check: 0.931 is below the throttling-only limit 0.949, so this steam could not have been tested with the throttling calorimeter alone, which is exactly why the combined unit is used.

bank.q: With the help of the psychrometric chart, explain sensible heating, sensible cooling, cooling and dehumidification, and evaporative (adiabatic) cooling of moist air. Give one air-conditioning use of each.
outline: Sensible heating: horizontal line, humidity ratio constant, DBT and enthalpy rise; winter heater
Sensible cooling: horizontal line to the left, above the dew point; coil above dew point
Cooling and dehumidification: the line bends down along the saturation curve, both DBT and w fall; summer coil below dew point
Evaporative cooling: nearly constant wet-bulb (enthalpy) line, DBT falls and w rises; desert cooler
Apparatus dew point and bypass factor as extra detail
answer: The chart: dry-bulb temperature across, humidity ratio w up, the saturation curve on top; lines of constant enthalpy and wet-bulb temperature slope down to the right. Values below use 101.325 kPa, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K) for air and h = 1.005T + w(2500 + 1.86T) per kg of dry air.

Sensible heating: air passes over a dry heater, w stays fixed, the point moves right, φ falls. Air at 15 °C and w = 0.008 heated to 30 °C needs q = (1.005 + 1.86 × 0.008) × 15 = 1.0199 × 15 = 15.3 kJ/kg dry air. Use: a winter room heater.

Sensible cooling: a coil whose surface is above the dew point; w stays fixed, the point moves left, φ rises. Air at state A (30 °C, w = 0.01605, dew point 21.4 °C) cooled to 24 °C gives up q = (1.005 + 1.86 × 0.01605) × 6 = 1.0349 × 6 = 6.2 kJ/kg dry air. Use: a chilled-beam ceiling that must stay dry.

Cooling and dehumidification: a coil below the dew point. The air cools along constant w to 21.4 °C, then follows the saturation curve as water condenses. Cooling A to saturated air at 14 °C: w₂ = 0.622 × 1.599/(101.325 − 1.599) = 0.00997; h₂ = 1.005 × 14 + 0.00997 × 2526.0 = 39.3 kJ/kg; h₁ = 71.2 kJ/kg.

For that coil: condensate = 0.01605 − 0.00997 = 0.00608 kg per kg dry air; heat removed q = h₁ − h₂ − Δw h<sub>f</sub>(14 °C) = 71.2 − 39.3 − 0.00608 × 58.8 = 31.6 kJ/kg dry air. Use: every summer split air-conditioner coil in Chennai.

Evaporative cooling: air passes over wet pads; water evaporates using the air’s own heat, so h (and nearly the wet-bulb temperature) stays constant while T falls and w rises. Air at 40 °C and 20 % (p<sub>v</sub> = 1.477 kPa, w = 0.00920, h = 63.9 kJ/kg) cooled to 28 °C at constant h reaches w = (63.9 − 28.14)/2552.1 = 0.01401, about 59 % RH, evaporating 0.0048 kg of water per kg of dry air. Use: a desert cooler in dry North Indian summers.

answer: Extra detail for the dehumidifying coil: the coil surface temperature is the apparatus dew point; the bypass factor is the fraction of air that passes the coil untouched, so the leaving state lies on the line from A to the apparatus dew point.
Check: in every process the energy balance closes; for the evaporative cooler, 1.005 × 28 + 0.01401 × (2500 + 1.86 × 28) = 28.14 + 35.75 = 63.9 kJ/kg, the same enthalpy as at entry.

bank.q: Compare steam tables, the Mollier chart and a throttling calorimeter as ways of obtaining the enthalpy of wet steam in a plant trial. State the accuracy, speed and range of each and recommend one for a routine boiler test.
outline: Tables: most accurate inside the printed range, interpolation needed, slow by hand
Mollier chart: fast for combined processes and expansions, reading error of several kJ/kg
Calorimeter: measures the actual steam in the pipe, so it finds the real x, but needs dry-enough steam and good instruments
Recommendation: calorimeter for x, tables for the other properties, chart for sketching the process
Sources of error: heat loss in the throttle, kinetic energy, gauge errors, interpolation
answer: The problem: the enthalpy of wet steam is h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub>. Tables and charts supply h<sub>f</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> at the measured pressure, but neither can tell the dryness x of the steam actually in the pipe; that needs a measurement.

Steam tables: values of IAPWS quality, so the error is set by interpolation. Interpolating 10 bar between 250 °C and 300 °C for 280 °C gave 3008.2 kJ/kg against 3008.6 kJ/kg tabulated, an error of 0.4 kJ/kg. Slow by hand but the most accurate.

Mollier chart: fast, and a whole expansion is a single line (10 bar, 250 °C to 1 bar at constant s gave Δh = 429.4 kJ/kg). A by-eye reading carries several kJ/kg of error, and a misread line can cost far more (the 225 °C isotherm instead of 250 °C gives 2887 instead of 2943 kJ/kg).

Throttling calorimeter: it measures the real steam, including carry-over from the drum, which no table can know. The sample outlet at 1 bar and 130 °C gave x = 0.980 at 10 bar. Its range is limited to x above about 0.95 (0.949 at 10 bar); wetter steam needs a combined separating and throttling unit.

Error sources in the calorimeter: heat loss from the throttle body (makes h₂ low and x low), kinetic energy left in the jet, a sample tube that does not catch droplets in proportion, and gauge errors. A 1 K error in T₂ changes x by only about 0.001, so temperature is not the weak point.

head: Method
Accuracy
Speed
Range
Gives x?
rows: x to about ±0.001 per K of T₂

answer: Recommendation for a routine boiler test: measure x with a throttling calorimeter (with a separator ahead of it if the steam may be wetter than 95 per cent), take h<sub>f</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> from the tables at the measured pressure, and use the chart only to sketch and check the process.

Worked figure: with x = 0.980 at 10 bar, h = 762.5 + 0.980 × 2014.6 = 762.5 + 1974.3 = 2736.8 kJ/kg, which matches h₂ = 2736.7 kJ/kg read at the calorimeter outlet, as the throttling balance requires.

bank.q: Saturated steam at 150 °C has p<sub>sat</sub> = 4.762 bar and v<sub>g</sub> = 0.3925 m³/kg. Compute the specific volume from pv = RT, find Z, and judge whether the ideal gas law can be used for steam near saturation.
outline: R for steam = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K, T = 423.15 K, p = 476.2 kPa
Ideal v = RT/p = 0.4101 m³/kg
The ideal law overstates v by about 4.5 %
Acceptable for rough work at low pressure, not when h or mass flow must be accurate; use tables near the dome
answer: Compressibility factor: Z = v<sub>actual</sub>/v<sub>ideal</sub> = 0.3925/0.4101 = 0.957.
Error: the ideal law overstates the volume by (0.4101 − 0.3925)/0.3925 = 4.5 per cent; in mass-flow terms it would understate the steam a pipe carries by about the same amount.

answer.text: The error grows as saturation pressure rises and vanishes for superheated steam at low pressure (values from the steam tables):

answer: Why: near the dome the molecules are close to condensing, so their attraction is strong and Z falls below 1. Far into the superheated region at low pressure they are far apart and Z → 1, as the compressibility chart shows.
The generalized chart is also weak here, because water is a polar molecule (its measured Z<sub>c</sub> is 0.229, against about 0.29 for simple gases), so tables are the right tool near the dome.

Judgement: pv = RT is acceptable for steam only as a rough estimate at low pressure or high superheat (for example, water vapour in moist air at a few kPa, where psychrometry uses it). For boiler, turbine or pipe sizing near saturation, use steam tables.
Check: Z × v<sub>ideal</sub> = 0.957 × 0.4101 = 0.3925 m³/kg, the table value.

bank.q: State the Gibbs phase rule, derive it by counting variables and equations, and apply it to water at the triple point, on the boiling curve and as superheated vapour, and to moist air over liquid water.
outline: F = C − P + 2 for a non-reacting system in equilibrium
Unknowns: T, p and C − 1 mole fractions per phase
Equations: equal chemical potential of each component in every phase, C(P − 1)
Water: F = 0 at the triple point, 1 on the boiling curve, 2 as superheated vapour
Moist air over water: C = 2, P = 2, F = 2
answer: Statement: for a system in equilibrium without chemical reactions, F = C − P + 2, where F is the number of intensive properties that can be varied independently, C the number of components and P the number of phases.
Unknowns: temperature and pressure, common to all phases (2), and in each phase C mole fractions of which only C − 1 are free, so P(C − 1). Total 2 + P(C − 1).
Equations: in equilibrium each component has the same chemical potential (Gibbs function per mole) in every phase, which gives P − 1 equations per component and C(P − 1) in all.
Four phases of water would give F = −1, which is impossible, so a pure substance has at most three phases in equilibrium.

Moist air over liquid water: C = 2 (dry air, water), P = 2 (gas, liquid), F = 2. Choosing T = 30 °C and p = 101.325 kPa uses both, so the air must be saturated: p<sub>v</sub> = p<sub>sat</sub>(30 °C) = 4.247 kPa and w = 0.622 × 4.247/97.078 = 0.0272 kg/kg.
The rule counts intensive properties only: for wet steam F = 1, yet the dryness fraction (an amount) is still needed to fix v, h and s.
Check: the triple point must give F = 0, and 1 − 3 + 2 = 0; the formula passes.

glossary.def: Another name for dryness fraction; the vapour mass fraction in a saturated liquid-vapour mixture.
Heat that changes the temperature of a single phase without changing the phase, equal to m·c·ΔT for a constant specific heat.
The difference between the actual temperature of superheated steam and the saturation temperature at the same pressure.
The amount by which a liquid is cooler than its saturation temperature at the given pressure.
The boiling or condensing temperature that belongs to a given pressure for a pure substance.
The pressure at which a pure substance boils at a given temperature.
A mixture of saturated liquid droplets and saturated vapour in equilibrium, with 0 < x < 1.
Steam with x = 1, containing no liquid droplets, at the saturation temperature for its pressure.
Steam above its saturation temperature for the given pressure; it behaves roughly as a gas.
h<sub>fg</sub>, the heat needed to convert 1 kg of saturated liquid into saturated vapour at constant pressure.
A gas whose behaviour departs from pv = RT because its molecules have volume and interact.
p<sub>r</sub> = p/p<sub>c</sub>, the pressure divided by the critical pressure of the substance.
T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>, the absolute temperature divided by the critical temperature.
All substances at the same reduced pressure and temperature have nearly the same compressibility factor Z.
The volume of an ideal gas mixture equals the sum of the volumes each component would occupy at the mixture pressure and temperature.
The pressure a single component of a gas mixture would exert if it alone filled the same volume at the same temperature.
Air with the water vapour removed; it is the reference mass for humidity ratio calculations.
φ = p<sub>v</sub>/p<sub>sat</sub> at the dry-bulb temperature, the ratio of actual vapour pressure to the saturation value.
The temperature at which moist air becomes saturated when cooled at constant pressure and humidity ratio.
The ordinary temperature of moist air measured by a thermometer with a dry bulb.
The temperature reached by a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in wet cloth and exposed to moving air.
A steady-flow expansion through a restriction with no work and negligible heat transfer, so enthalpy stays constant.
The number of intensive properties that can be varied independently without changing the number of phases; F in the Gibbs phase rule.
One of the smallest set of chemical species needed to make up every phase of a system; water is one component, moist air two.
μ = w/w<sub>s</sub>, the humidity ratio divided by that of saturated air at the same temperature and pressure.
A substance above both its critical temperature and critical pressure, where liquid and vapour cannot be told apart.
